Let's dive into Chapter 1: Understanding Racism as Choices, Not Identity.
You know, it’s easy to think of racism as something far away—maybe it belongs to other people, or it’s just part of history. But here’s the thing: the line between being racist and being antiracist isn’t some fixed border. It’s drawn and redrawn every day, shaped by the choices we make, the words we use, the policies we support, and even the moments when we choose to stay silent.
For a lot of us, this realization doesn’t hit all at once. It’s more like a slow, sometimes awkward awakening.
Imagine a teenager in a packed high school auditorium. Their heart’s pounding—they’re about to give a speech for Black History Month. On the surface, the words are meant to inspire and challenge injustice. But underneath, there’s this quiet anxiety: Are these words enough? Are they the right ones? The speech draws on lessons from teachers and family, filled with hope and pride, but it also carries the weight of stereotypes and half-truths picked up from the world around them.
When the applause dies down, that young speaker feels both proud and uneasy. Something about what they said just doesn’t sit right. It’s only later, looking back, that the contradictions become clear. The speech had praised hard work as the answer to racial inequality—echoing this idea that if people just try harder, they can overcome any barrier. But that message, as comforting as it sounds, quietly puts the blame on those who struggle, ignoring the massive obstacles built into the system itself.
And honestly, most of us don’t notice how easily those ideas sneak into our everyday thinking. It’s tempting to believe racism is just about “bad” people doing “bad” things, while everyone else is neutral. But here’s something to pay attention to: neutrality is a myth. Every belief, every action, every policy either supports the old hierarchies or challenges them. There’s no truly safe middle ground.
This understanding doesn’t show up overnight. It grows in those uncomfortable moments—like hearing a family member repeat a stereotype, noticing who gets stopped by security at the mall, or realizing which neighborhoods are called “good” or “bad.” Each of these moments is a chance to choose: do you go along with the status quo, or do you stop and question it?
Being antiracist isn’t a permanent badge you earn. It’s a series of choices, made over and over. And it all starts with self-examination—not just saying “I’m not racist,” but asking, in each situation, am I supporting equality, or am I propping up injustice?
This isn’t easy work. It means looking honestly at your own mistakes, unlearning old habits, and being open to change. But really, that’s the only way forward.
Racism isn’t just about personal prejudice—it’s woven into our laws, our schools, our workplaces, and our neighborhoods. Being antiracist means seeing that, and being willing to change not just minds and hearts, but also the systems that shape our lives every day.
It’s a process, not a finish line. And it all begins with the courage to see things just as they are.
